newsitem.title: JAPAN: Behind angry words N.Korea comes out of isolation.
newsitem.headline: Behind angry words N.Korea comes out of isolation.

text.p: Whenever a gun goes off on the demilitarised zone separating North and South Korea, the two nations exchange angry words at each other and the world waits.

Pyongyang's propaganda machine issues dire warnings of what could happen to all and sundry while Seoul says a DMZ clash is the latest sign of North Korea's desperate situation so the world should watch out.
But behind the fire and brimstone words, there appear to be growing signs that while the threat is still real, the world may not need to hold its breath quite as anxiously any more.
Take Wednesday's latest incident in the DMZ when the two countries accused each other of starting a brief firefight in which North Korea says several of its soldiers were wounded.

The incident did not develop and only hours after it, North Korea was taking a major step towards thawing ties with one of South Korea's main allies, Japan, by announcing Japanese wives living there could return to their homeland for the first time in decades.

Most of the estimated 1,800 women married their husbands in Japan and followed them to North Korea between 1959 and 1982. But they were stranded as relations soured between the two countries, which at present have no diplomatic relations.
"We must welcome the North Korean announcement," Japanese government spokesman Kaoru Yosano told a news conference.

Even the U.S. State Department played down the latest clash, saying while it was unusually provocative, they do not expect it to derail food aid to famine-hit North Korea or efforts to bring North Korea into peace talks.
North Korea watchers caution there is always a chance that a minor border incident could flare into a major conflict.

But as growing numbers of western officials visit North Korea, the analysts see more and more signs that the hardline Stalinist nation is ending its isolation and slowly starting to part the bamboo curtain that has cut it off for so long.

Even on the eve of Wednesday's clash, a team of 10 U.S. experts had just arrived in North Korea on Tuesday to begin joint search and recovery operations for remains of Americans missing in action from the 1950-53 Korean War.

Four-way peace talks involving the United States, North Korea, South Korea and China are less than one month away and in its denunciation of Wednesday's clash North Korea made no mention of linking it to the negotiations.

In other positive developments on the immediate horizon, Japan and North Korea reopen low-level talks on the weekend about their relations after nearly a three-month gap and at the same time two senior U.S. emissaries arrive in Pyongyang.

The emissaries are former U.S. Senator Sam Nunn, who once headed the Senate Armed Services Committee and is a respected American voice on national security issues, and James Laney, who has just retired as U.S. ambassador to South Korea.
Some North Korea watchers said the enmity between North and South Korea was now being driven as much by both countries domestic political concerns as big power politics.
They said North Korean leader King Jong-il always has a convenient rallying cry for his people as they struggle through a desperate famine by raising the spectre of an attack by the rival south.

In the same vein, as South Korea heads into a presidential campaign at the end of this year and copes with scandals hitting the present Seoul government, the ever-present threat of a North Korean attack is guaranteed to capture headlines.
